newsitem.title: UK: British shops have patchy Christmas.
newsitem.headline: British shops have patchy Christmas.

text.p: A surprise profit warning from catalogue stores group Argos Plc on Friday showed that Christmas was a mixed bag for British retailers, and not the runaway spending splurge many had hoped for.
Argos's downbeat comments sent retail stocks into a tailspin as expectations for a bumper festive season for store owners looked increasingly overoptimistic.

Argos shares fell more than 15 percent to 620.5 pence, down 112.5 pence. Fashion retailer Next Plc was 24 pence lower at 527.5, Marks and Spencer Plc was 16 pence down at 466.5 pence and Great Universal Stores Plc down 22 pence to 580.5 pence.
"Having expected reasonably good trading the market has become unsettled by Argos's comments," said Rodney Forest, retail analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
"It's a very different picture depending on the retailer," he said, "Overall sales have been disappointing compared to demanding expectations."
The picture emerging was one of winners and losers, with big ticket consumer durables doing better than fashion, footwear, toys and gifts, analysts said.
"Christmas was patchy...not every retailer enjoyed the benefit of increased sales," said Clive Vaughan at retail analysts Verdict. "People had expected a boom and they've not got a boom."
A survey on Friday by Britain's Confederation of British Industry found that Christmas retail sales were higher than the same month last year, but growth fell well below expectations.
The report showed the winners in December were booksellers and stationers, grocers, confectioners and specialist food stores. Footwear and leather shops were hit hardest.

Analysts suggested pre-election uncertainty and general worries about job security may have restrained spending. Older, more affluent shoppers were probably driving the demand for durables, some of it replacement, while the less well-off were more reluctant to splash out even on low-cost items.

Argos, one of the success stories of the 1990s retail scene, said additional costs and lower than expected sales meant full year profits were unlikely to exceed the lowest of market expectations, currently 140 million pounds ($235 million).

Dixons Group Plc, which saw sales up eight percent in the eight weeks including Christmas, clearly benefited from shoppers' appetite for personal computers, televisions and mobile phones. But the sales increase was still below market expectations, which had hoped for growth of around 10 percent, retail analysts said.

A gloomy report on Thursday from Sears Plc, the beleaguered shoes-to-Selfridges retail empire, aroused fears for other clothing and footwear sellers Next and market leader Marks and Spencer, who have yet to give their verdict on Christmas.

But privately-held group the John Lewis Partnership JLP.CN said its department store sales jumped 31.7 percent in the week to January 4. The firm did say however that the figures were influenced by the the January sale falling a week later than the comparable time last year.

Britain's biggest jewellery retailer Signet Group Plc, the re-named Ratners, had a good Christmas, with comparable store sales up 8.6 percent in the four weeks to December 28. Analysts said its success could have made life tough for Argos, the country's second biggest in jewellery.
And greeting card group Clinton Cards Plc said it would beat profit forecasts after buoyant pre-Christmas sales. ($1=.5950 Pound)
